scope: It was my family in Jakarta: what they pay for groceries, fuel and the basics of daily life, and their rupiah savings for retirement.
The fear runs like a chain.
Three months after a shock, the rupiah was 5 percent or more weaker in two of six.
Foreign investors pulled money out around four of six past shocks.
Prices kept rising after six of six sharp falls in the rupiah, but inflation sped up by 2 percentage points or more after one of six.
By my tests, the foreign-money link holds; the other links do not.
I used Indonesia's own history and fixed the rules in a pre-registration on GitHub, with later changes dated.
Their rules were fixed before I read the rate data, but not before I knew the broad outline of Indonesia's economic history.
So before reading that data I wrote down what I expected for each comparison.
Twenty-two of the twenty-two predictions I could check came true, so read the savings and borrowing results as confirming what an attentive reader could have guessed, not as discoveries.
An episode counts for a link only once its outcome is known.
The fear starts in the markets, so I keep this part short.
By August 2026, the index stood 20.8 percent below its level before that shock, on Bank Indonesia's preliminary figures; at the 16 October close, it stood 37.0 percent below.
In January, MSCI froze its index rebalancing for Indonesian shares over concerns about free float (Sigit, 2026), and on 28 January 2026 the IHSG closed 7.35 percent lower.
Three months after the shock month, the rupiah was 5 percent or more weaker against the US dollar in two of six episodes: after September 2008, by 19.7 percent, and after March 2026, by 6.6 percent.

In the episode that began in March 2026, the outflow came to US$4.0 billion over those quarters, and in the weeks OJK files under January to September 2026, foreign investors sold a net Rp82 trillion of Indonesian shares on the exchange.
BPS's own published rates, as Bank Indonesia reports them (Bank Indonesia, 2026a), differ by as much as 0.8 percentage points from the figures I computed and give the same count.
Across the 261 twelve-month periods starting from January 2004, the same deposit lost buying power in 34 percent.

Bank Indonesia's policy rate (for May 2004, the one-month SBI rate) rose by 0.25 percentage points or more in the slide month or the three months after in two of the five slides I could check, after 2008 and 2013; for 2005, I could not find its rate for July.

| The fear | My test | Result | By my test | |---|---|---|---| | Stocks crash and stay down | Still below the pre-shock level a year later | One of five | Does not hold | | The rupiah falls | 5 percent weaker three months on | Two of six | Does not hold | | Foreign investors leave | Net outflow over the shock's quarter and the next | Four of six | Holds | | Inflation speeds up | 2 points faster over the year after a slide | One of six | Does not hold | | Savings lose buying power | A deposit, after tax, behind prices | Two of six | Does not hold | | Borrowing gets dearer | Consumer-loan rate a point higher a year on | One of six | Does not hold | | Unemployment rises | Not tested (see the limits) | | |
The stock market can keep falling, and foreign money is already leaving Indonesian shares.
Faster inflation, a deposit's lost buying power and dearer loans followed past slides in a minority of cases, and the rupiah has not slid so far.
It is the price of fuel: within months of the single slide after which inflation sped up by 2 percentage points or more, the government raised fuel prices sharply.

Bank Indonesia's earlier month-end figures failed a check against the exchange's own records, so the 1997 crash is in the price and savings tests but not in the stock tests. - March 2008 barely counts as a shock: the index fell 10.1 percent that month, against a threshold of 10 percent. - The slide rule has another reading.
Read as I fixed it, slides in the few years that followed join the 1997 episode; cut at the end of that crisis instead, the link does not hold. - I could not test jobs.

Shock months use the IHSG's month-end close: Bank Indonesia's statistics table III.3 from December 2005 (Bank Indonesia, 2026c), Bapepam's capital market statistics before that (Badan Pengawas Pasar Modal, 2005), and six months corrected to the Indonesia Stock Exchange's own figures (Indonesia Stock Exchange, 2007; Indonesia Stock Exchange, 2009; Indonesia Stock Exchange, 2021) or Bapepam-LK's (Badan Pengawas Pasar Modal dan Lembaga Keuangan, 2007).
Each month from December 2005 was checked against an independent publication.

Prices are the International Monetary Fund's headline consumer price index for Indonesia, compiled by BPS-Statistics Indonesia (International Monetary Fund, 2026b), set beside BPS's published rates from Bank Indonesia's inflation data (Bank Indonesia, 2026a).
Fuel price changes come from government regulations and official notices, each stored and checked by script.

[README.md] The first four tests were fixed before any outcome was computed; the savings and borrowing tests were added after those results; their rules were fixed before the rate data was read, but not before the broad outline of Indonesia's economic history was known, and predictions were written down first, as the pre-registration records.

[README.md] A year after a shock, the IHSG was back above its pre-shock level in four of five episodes; the rupiah was 5 percent or more weaker three months on after two of six; inflation sped up by 2 percentage points or more after one of six rupiah slides; a one-month bank deposit lost buying power after tax after two of six; and the consumer-loan rate rose a point or more after one of six.

[README.md] The data files are not in the repository; `data/README.md` says where each file the build reads comes from.
[data/README.md] Each data file `build_analysis.py` reads is frozen by its SHA-256, which it checks before reading it; a fresh download may differ and then needs a new vet.

[data/README.md] Six months are corrected to the Indonesia Stock Exchange's own statistics or Bapepam-LK's statistics by `extract_ihsg_corrections.py` (Indonesia Stock Exchange files cited with their access date, as its terms require). - **Rupiah per US dollar, daily.** Bank for International Settlements, US dollar exchange rates (data.bis.org, topic XRU, series for Indonesia), with its national sources: the US Federal Reserve, then the European Central Bank.

[data/README.md] Inflation rates are the author's calculations. - **Context.** OJK's Portal Data SJK Terintegrasi: the daily IHSG and weekly foreign trading on the exchange. - **Deposit, loan and policy rates, monthly.** Bank Indonesia, SEKI Tables I.28 (rupiah time-deposit rates), I.26 (rupiah loan rates) and I.25.A (policy and money-market rates), commercial banks as a whole (bi.go.id, statistics, SEKI); credited to Bank Indonesia.

[data/README.md] Each was checked against an earlier edition of the same table archived by the Internet Archive. - **BPS's published inflation, monthly.** Bank Indonesia's Data Inflasi page (bi.go.id, statistics, indicators), which reports BPS's year-on-year headline inflation; downloaded by hand. - **Deposit interest tax.** Government Regulations PP 131/2000 and PP 51/1994, from peraturan.bpk.go.id; PP 131/2000's rate is bound to a stored quote in `docs/sources.json`. - **Fuel price changes.** Government regulations and official notices from peraturan.bpk.go.id, the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources (esdm.go.id, migas.esdm.go.id, its legal documentation site) and Pertamina, many through Internet Archive copies; `extract_fuel.py` checks each passage in `docs/fuel-manifest.csv` against the stored document and writes `fuel_price_changes.csv`. - **The October fall.** Indonesia Stock Exchange, IDX Daily Statistics for 16 October 2026 and the trading day before (idx.co.id, Market Data, Statistical Reports, Daily), downloaded by hand and read by `extract_idx_daily.py`; cited with the access date, as the exchange's terms require.

[data/README.md] - OECD's monthly share price series for Indonesia names a commercial website as its source and averages daily closes, so it was not used. - Bank Indonesia's table places the year label on the first month of each year in older sheets and on the last month in recent years; the reader groups each year's months instead of carrying the label forward. - The Indonesia Stock Exchange's terms forbid scraping; its statistics were read from individual documents. - MSCI's terms bar use of its content with language models without a licence, so MSCI's own documents were not used; its announcement is reported from the press. - BPS's site blocks Anthropic's crawler in its robots file, so BPS's own pages and tables were not used, and the unemployment test could not be run: no other official source with BPS's round-by-round figures could be used.

[data/README.md] Kompas bans AI use in its robots file and was not used. - Bank Indonesia's rate tables spread each series over several sheets, label the year on a few months in newer sheets, and Table I.26 repeats December 2018 (the first copy empty); `seki.py` checks each case. - From 2015 the Premium price the government set applied outside Java, Madura and Bali; the Java price, set by Pertamina, was verified for January 2016 alone, so the other Premium rows from 2015 on are listed as size not verified.
